content: The composition of influenza vaccines must be determined several months before the start of each flu season. This timeline ensures there is sufficient time for the manufacturing and distribution of the vaccines. The selection of vaccine strains is based on global influenza surveillance data, which helps identify the viruses most likely to circulate in the upcoming season. However, due to antigenic drift in influenza A viruses or changes in the predominant lineage of influenza B viruses, the circulating viruses during a season may differ from those included in the vaccine. Such mismatches can influence the effectiveness of seasonal influenza vaccines. When there is a good match between the vaccine strains and the circulating viruses, increased protection has been observed. This includes reduced influenza-associated emergency department visits and hospitalizations among older adults, decreased influenza-like illness (ILI) in younger working adults, and lower rates of laboratory-confirmed influenza (LCI) in observational studies. Even in seasons with suboptimal matches, influenza vaccines have been shown to provide some level of protection against influenza and related outcomes, such as hospitalizations. In addition to antigenic drift in circulating viruses, vaccine viruses may undergo adaptive mutations during propagation in eggs. These mutations can lead to antigenic differences between the vaccine virus and the circulating virus, potentially reducing vaccine effectiveness. The composition of influenza vaccines is updated annually, with one or more vaccine strains replaced to protect against anticipated circulating viruses. Evidence from clinical trials suggests that protection against antigenically similar viruses lasts at least 6–8 months, particularly in non-elderly populations. In some cases, immunity may persist longer if circulating virus strains remain antigenically similar across multiple seasons. For example, the 1968 pandemic vaccine demonstrated 67% effectiveness in preventing influenza caused by the A/Hong Kong/68 virus. Serum hemagglutination inhibition (HAI) antibodies elicited by vaccination have been detected in children vaccinated with live attenuated influenza vaccine (LAIV) for over a year post-vaccination. In one community-based trial, children who received a single dose of LAIV3 in the previous season showed continued protection against influenza during the following season. A review of four trials involving young children aged 6 months to 18 years reported that the efficacy of LAIV3 against influenza A (H1N1) and A (H3N2) was similar at 9–12 months post-vaccination compared to 1–5 months post-vaccination. For influenza B strains, efficacy remained comparable at 5–7 months post-vaccination. Additionally, two randomized trials and one open-label study reported residual efficacy through a second season without revaccination, though at lower levels than observed in the first season. Recent observational studies have attempted to evaluate changes in influenza vaccine effectiveness over the course of a single season. Some studies have noted a decline in vaccine effectiveness, particularly against influenza A (H3N2) viruses, with the most pronounced reductions observed among older adults. However, this effect has not been consistently observed across all age groups and seasons. Factors such as increased circulation of antigenically drifted variants during the season may partially explain these findings. These issues are discussed in greater detail in the section on the timing of vaccination.
